summary:
Kerala is a state within India and stands under the national transgender-rights framework, which Parliament narrowed in March 2026. The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill replaced the 2019 law's self-identification route with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist; the government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking, while critics say it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

The national baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court of India in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, which courts have interpreted to cover gender identity: the Supreme Court has held that discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity falls within Article 15's prohibition of discrimination by sex, and the Allahabad High Court extended that in 2021 to bar employment discrimination on sexual orientation grounds. There is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed legal safeguards that had protected trans persons from sexual violence, and trans people fear a rise in assaults because the new code omits the gender-identity-specific offences the old law carried.

Identity documents and checkpoints are a live source of friction across the country. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person who had been asked to take a medical exam by passport authorities. In November 2024 an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, was stopped at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 by Central Industrial Security Force personnel despite presenting her PAN card. In Kolkata a transwoman alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her at the station under the pretext of checking her gender, and transgender persons arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam have recounted degrading treatment in custody.

Assessments of police conduct diverge. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic; victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy, with directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. Bans flowing from that judgment and from the National Medical Commission in 2022 coexist with clandestine networks still operating.

Kerala's own enforcement record under the national statute is among the highest sub-national totals in India. A crime-data report of 30 January 2026 records two of the seven national Transgender Persons Act cases in 2021 as arising in Kerala, and four of the eleven in 2023, a figure joint-highest with Tamil Nadu. The report cautions that national counts are tiny because of police-registration bias, so these totals measure recorded cases rather than incidence.

Facilities and care access are set largely at state level. The Union government told Parliament in December 2021 that Kerala is among twelve states and union territories reported to have constituted Transgender Welfare Boards under Section 10(1) of the 2019 Rules. Kerala's board operates alongside those of Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra and Odisha, coordinating housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pensions. Nationally, the Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community, and in August 2024 the Ministry of Finance clarified that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries.

Intersex minors remain at risk. Reports document a history of infanticide and a strong parental preference for assigning intersex infants male through non-consensual operations, and the Madras High Court ordered Tamil Nadu in April 2019 to ban sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants.
tangentialFactors:
Kerala's four recorded Transgender Persons Act cases in 2023 put it level with Tamil Nadu at the top of the state-level table, while the national total for that year was eleven. The gap between a handful of registered cases and an estimated two million transgender people nationwide is attributed by the crime-data report to police-registration bias, which means formal complaint counts understate violence rather than rebut it.

The narrow recognition scheme introduced nationally in March 2026 is a country-wide condition rather than a Kerala-specific one, as are the 2024 replacement of the Indian Penal Code by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita and the absence of same-sex marriage or civil partnership. Complaints about document and checkpoint friction are documented in several states, including airport stops in Tamil Nadu, railway encounters in West Bengal and Assam, and passport-authority medical examinations challenged before the Allahabad High Court.

Police conduct assessments differ by source and period. A foreign government's December 2025 country policy note describes limited, non-systemic abuse likelier in conservative rural areas, whereas victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. Court-ordered protections and conversion-therapy bans issued by the Madras High Court in 2021 and by the National Medical Commission in 2022 have not ended clandestine practice.
localsOnly:
Kerala residents have access to a Transgender Welfare Board constituted under Section 10(1) of the 2019 Rules, one of twelve such bodies reported to Parliament in December 2021. The board coordinates housing subsidies, sex reassignment surgery provided free in public hospitals and pensions, in common with the arrangements run by Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra and Odisha.

Resident-level healthcare coverage widened in April 2024, when the Ayushman Bharat scheme was extended to transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community. Since August 2024 the Ministry of Finance has confirmed that LGBTQ people may open joint bank accounts and name partners as beneficiaries without restriction.

Legal recourse for residents rests on Article 15 as interpreted by the Supreme Court of India to cover discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity, and on the employment discrimination bar extended by the Allahabad High Court in 2021. The Madras High Court's guidelines of 7 June 2021 direct police sensitisation, protection of LGBTQIA+ persons and a ban on conversion therapy, with directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities.

Residents who report through the police feed the statistics on which state-level comparisons rest; Kerala registered two of the seven national Transgender Persons Act cases in 2021 and four of the eleven in 2023.
outOfScopeNotes:
The crime-data report of 30 January 2026 states its own caveat that national counts are small because of police-registration bias, so whether Kerala's high share reflects higher incidence or higher reporting is unresolved on the sources available here.

No source in this inventory documents enforcement of the March 2026 recognition amendment within Kerala, including how the state treats trans men, trans women or non-binary residents who self-identify outside the recognised socio-cultural categories. Whether the Kerala Transgender Welfare Board has been reconstituted, re-scoped or funded differently after that amendment is also not sourced here.

No Kerala-specific incident of violence against a trans person, with a date, location and outcome, is documented in this inventory. The 2026 crime-data figures give case counts only, without charges, dispositions or sentences. Claims about clandestine conversion-therapy networks are national and undated as to Kerala.
